newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis rally for peace on eve of Netanyahu visit.
newsitem.headline: Israelis rally for peace on eve of Netanyahu visit.

text.p: Thousands of Israelis attended a pro-peace rally in Tel Aviv on Saturday night ahead of a visit to Washington by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to discuss the faltering Israeli-Palestinian peace process.
Netanyahu could face pressure from U.S. President Bill Clinton at a meeting at the White House on Monday to make a gesture that would help talks to resume.
Palestinian official Hanan Ashrawi said she will fly on Sunday to Washington where she will meet with U.S. administration officials on behalf of Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
"The purpose of my visit is to meet with the American administration...and to present the Palestinian point of view in terms of settlements and Jerusalem," Ashrawi told Reuters.
Earlier on Saturday Palestinian officials warned of a "comprehensive explosion" in the peace process which could lead to more confrontations and said they were sending a message to Clinton.

Israel's ground breaking of a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem last month triggered daily Palestinian clashes with Israeli troops, halted peace talks and angered the rest of the Arab world.
In Tel Aviv, thousands of Israelis gathered at the square where Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated on November 4, 1995 by a right-Jew opposed to his peace policies with the Arabs.

In an address to the assembly, Israeli opposition leader Shimon Peres slammed the policies of Netanyahu, who ousted Peres in the national election last May, and called for an immediate resumption of peace talks.
"We want to continue in the path of Yitzhak Rabin, a path of peace," said Oren Yehishalom, one of the organisers.

Netanyahu has rejected the original basis of the Middle East peace talks: Israel trading occupied Arab land for peace with its Arab neighbours. In advance of his trip to Washington, he also emphasised his intention to continue building Jewish settlements on occupied Arab land.
But amid the crisis he has proposed rapid 'final status' negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians to wind up in six months, instead of the original 1999 deadline.
If the talks bog down he suggested a Camp David style summit -- along the lines of the one that produced Israel's peace agreement with Egypt in 1978 -- between himself, Arafat and Clinton.

Palestinians, in a weak position and fearing existing agreements will not be implemented, have said Israel must stop work on the new Jerusalem settlement before Arafat will meet Netanyahu. The rightwing Israeli leader has vowed not to halt the settlement.

Israel, for its part, has demanded the Palestinian Authority crack down on "terrorism" as a condition for resuming peace talks. It has accued Arafat of giving a "green light" to resumed Islamic bombings against Israel.
Israel claims all of Jerusalem as its capital. The Palestinians want East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in 1967 along with the rest of the West Bank, as capital of a future state.

Palestinians see new Jewish settlement as an effort to pre-empt the negotiations they are supposed to hold on the future of East Jerusalem and the rest the West Bank and Gaza under agreements signed by the previous Israeli government.
